content: Listeriosis is a group of infectious diseases caused by bacteria of the genus Listeria, most commonly Listeria monocytogenes. This bacterium is a flagellated, catalase-positive, facultatively intracellular, anaerobic, Gram-positive bacillus. The incidence of listeriosis is approximately 3 cases per 100,000 individuals. Transmission typically occurs through the ingestion of contaminated food or via vertical transmission from mother to fetus. Once inside the human host, Listeria expresses thermoregulated virulence factors, invades the intestinal epithelium, and multiplies intracellularly within phagocytic phagolysosomes. It can escape lysosomal destruction by secreting phospholipases and listeriolysin O, a hemolysin that lyses the vacuole membrane. The bacterium then spreads between cells by forming actin-based protrusions called filopods or rockets. Listeria infections can manifest as various clinical syndromes, including neonatal listeriosis, genitourinary infections, gastroenteritis, central nervous system (CNS) infections, endocarditis, bacteremia, and localized infections. Risk factors for developing listeriosis include consuming uncooked meats and vegetables, unpasteurized milk and cheeses, processed or ready-to-eat meats, and smoked seafood. High-risk populations include transplant recipients, individuals with a history of splenectomy, those receiving immunosuppressive therapy, patients with advanced diabetes, kidney or liver disease, or active malignancy, as well as neonates, pregnant women, and the elderly. Most healthy individuals do not develop clinical symptoms or may experience mild, transient bacteremia. Early symptoms, such as fever, typically appear within 24 hours of transmission. If untreated, the disease can progress within 1 to 90 days to complications such as bacteremia, abscess formation, pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), acute kidney injury, and CNS impairment. Healthy children and young adults generally have a good prognosis, but high-risk populations are more likely to experience severe complications and death, even with prompt treatment. The diagnosis of listeriosis is confirmed by isolating Listeria monocytogenes from a normally sterile site, such as blood, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in cases of CNS involvement, or amniotic fluid/placenta in pregnancy-related cases. Cultures from non-sterile sites, such as stool, are not routinely recommended but may be useful in cases of gastroenteritis with high suspicion of listeriosis. Listeria can be readily isolated on routine media, but only one-third of cultures yield positive Gram stains due to its intracellular nature. Selective enrichment media can improve isolation rates from contaminated specimens. A negative culture does not rule out infection if clinical suspicion is high. MRI of the brain may be helpful in diagnosing CNS listeriosis, particularly when brainstem involvement is observed. All patients with listeriosis require antibiotic therapy. The treatment of choice is ampicillin, with or without gentamicin. For patients intolerant to penicillins, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole may be used. The duration of therapy depends on the clinical syndrome, ranging from several days for uncomplicated gastroenteritis to six weeks for endocarditis or encephalitis. Listerial gastroenteritis is often self-limited in healthy adults, but a short course of oral ampicillin may be considered for immunocompromised or pregnant individuals or those exposed to implicated food during outbreaks. Non-gastroenteritis listeriosis often requires hospitalization and intravenous antibiotic therapy. Surgery may be necessary for complications such as abscess drainage or advanced endocarditis requiring valve repair. Preventing listeriosis involves proper washing and handling of food, maintaining a clean and safe kitchen environment, thoroughly cooking meat and poultry, safely storing foods, and choosing safe food options. High-risk individuals, such as pregnant women, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals, should take additional precautions. There is no vaccine against listeriosis, and pharmacologic prophylaxis is not recommended. Historically, Listeria monocytogenes was first isolated in 1926 by Everitt Murray and renamed in 1940 in honor of Joseph Lister. Initially described as a bacterium affecting laboratory animals, the first human cases were reported in 1929 by Nyfeldt in Denmark. Listeriosis has a worldwide distribution, affecting both developed and developing countries.
